Chapter 1: The Birth of the Transistor
1947. Before silicon, there was germanium. Goal: build a transistor radio!
Ashes to Elements
Smelt coal into coal ash. Some coal deposits contain trace germanium.
Reduction
Reduce GeO2 with charcoal into metallic germanium. Still full of impurities - not nearly pure enough for a transistor!
Zone Refining
Refine germanium. A molten zone sweeps impurities to one end of the bar (Pfann, 1952).
The First Transistor
Two gold points on n-type germanium: the point-contact transistor (Bardeen and Brattain, 1947).
Music from Coal
Build a transistor radio. In 1954 this changed how the world listened.
Needle in a Haystack
Combine 8 coal ash into germanium concentrate. Only a tiny fraction is germanium.
Brimstone Chemistry
Burn sulfur powder in a furnace to get SO2, then dissolve it in water. Real plants oxidize SO2 to SO3 first (contact process).
Leaching
Dissolve the concentrate in acid to get germanium dioxide (GeO2).
Doping
Add a trace of phosphorus to make n-type germanium. Purify first, then add exactly the impurity you want.
The Sandwich
Indium on both sides of n-type germanium, then heat: a p-n-p alloy-junction transistor (1952).
tooltip.semiconductor-lab.purity.hint: Transistors need 9N or better. Zone refining raises purity one step at a time (up to 10N for Ge).
item.semiconductor-lab.fused_quartz.plac: Placeholder: quartz melts at ~1713°C; a furnace (~1000°C) cannot melt it. Will be replaced by the oxyhydrogen torch [7-02] (H2+O2, Gaudin 1839).
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: Molten germanium does not react with graphite. Silicon does (forms SiC) - which is why Chapter 2 needs a different method.
item.semiconductor-lab.quartz_tube.note: Fused silica (pure SiO2) survives high heat and adds no impurities. Ordinary glass would melt and leak sodium.
item.semiconductor-lab.induction_coil.no: High-frequency current in the coil heats only the germanium itself, melting a narrow zone. Real coils are water-cooled.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note: Moves the coil slowly along the bar. Too fast and impurities cannot keep up.
item.semiconductor-lab.electric_motor.no: Turns the lead screw. Real zone refiners move a few cm per hour.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite.note: Natural graphite from metamorphic rock (e.g. Sri Lanka vein graphite). Same stuff as pencil lead.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.not_ge: Only germanium can be zone-refined here. Put in reduced or refined germanium.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.max_pu: Already 11N - zone refining cannot go further.
message.semiconductor-lab.refiner.empty: The furnace is empty. Right-click with germanium to start.
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.hint: Left: Ge (max 8)  Mid: boat  Right: dopant
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.max: Now: %s (limit of zone refining). Add a dopant to make n/p-type
item.semiconductor-lab.refined_germanium: Purity is about the inside of the crystal. The surface gets dirty from your hands and air at once - real labs etch it off with acid (CP-4) right before use. Not yet in the game.
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.ready: Now: %s - transistor grade. Add a dopant, or refine to 10N
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.doping: Zone leveling: spreading dopant evenly through %s germanium
Made by zone leveling: dopant is added to the molten zone so it spreads evenly. Mixing solids would not work.

book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p1:
SEMICONDUCTOR LAB
Chapter 1: The Birth of the Transistor (1947)

Goal: build a transistor radio.

Everything here follows real chemistry. Where the game simplifies, this book says so.

Press L to see your next step.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p2:
1. GERMANIUM
Before silicon, there was germanium. It hides in two places: zinc ore (sphalerite, deep underground) and the ash of some coal.

Smelt coal for ash. Mine sphalerite with an iron pickaxe and roast it in a reverberatory furnace: every 4th gives germanium concentrate.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p3:
2. SULFURIC ACID
Burn sulfur powder (from sulfur caves) in a furnace: S + O2 -> SO2. Dissolve in water.

Simplified: real plants first oxidize SO2 to SO3 with a catalyst.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p4:
3. EXTRACT + REDUCE
Acid pulls germanium out of the concentrate as GeO2. Charcoal takes the oxygen away: metallic germanium, but still dirty.

Simplified: industry uses hydrogen, and chlorine distillation.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p5:
4. ZONE REFINING (Pfann, 1952)
Melt a narrow zone and move it along the bar. Impurities prefer the liquid, so they ride to the end.

Each pass: unrefined -> 6N -> 9N -> 10N. 9N = one impurity per billion atoms. 10N needs a synthetic graphite boat.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p6:
THE FURNACE
Graphite boat, quartz tube, copper induction coil, screw + motor.

HF oscillator (3 kW of electricity): 2 vacuum tubes + coil + Leyden jar. It ran on vacuum tubes!

Boat: clay-graphite = 9N max, synthetic graphite = 10N.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p7:
5. DOPING
Pure is not enough. Add ONE chosen impurity to the molten zone (zone leveling):
 phosphorus -> n-type (extra electrons)
 indium -> p-type (missing electrons)

Mixing solids would do nothing. Needs 9N or better.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p8:
6. TRANSISTORS
1947 point-contact: two gold needles on n-type Ge.
1952 alloy-junction: indium on both sides of n-type Ge, then heat -> p-n-p sandwich.

A small base current controls a large current. That is the whole trick.
book.semiconductor-lab.ch1.p9:
NO CLEAN ROOM?
Correct - in 1947 there were none. Laminar-flow clean rooms arrived in the 1960s, when one speck could kill a whole integrated circuit.

The surface of your germanium is dirty right now. Real labs etch it with acid before use.

block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Connected cables form one network: generators and discharging batteries feed machines directly (cables store nothing). Loss is 1% per cable along the longest path; at most 1 MW flows through a network, shared in proportion to demand. Right-click: network info.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnetite_ore.no: Fe3O4, the natural magnet (lodestone). Found deep in ancient banded iron formations.
block.semiconductor-lab.iron_sand.note: Magnetite grains washed out of rock and concentrated on beaches. Japanese tatara steel was made from this.
block.semiconductor-lab.wolframite_ore.n: (Fe,Mn)WO4. Forms in quartz veins at the edge of granite. 'Tungsten' is Swedish for 'heavy stone'.
block.semiconductor-lab.galena_ore.note: PbS. Forms with sphalerite in the same hydrothermal veins - look near zinc ore. Often carries silver.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnet.note: Magnetite that nature magnetized (lightning does it). Known since antiquity as lodestone.
item.semiconductor-lab.dynamo.note: Faraday 1831: spin a coil in a magnetic field and current flows. Early dynamos used permanent magnets; from 1866 (Siemens) the iron core's residual magnetism was enough.
block.semiconductor-lab.water_wheel.note: Needs FLOWING water beside it (500 W per side). Still water does nothing: power = flow x head. Early power stations were hydro.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_engine.not: Coal boils water, steam pushes a piston, the dynamo turns: 50 kW. Watt's engine converted only 2-5% of the coal's heat into work; ~30% only came with steam turbines. One water bucket = 2 coal's worth of steam.
block.semiconductor-lab.electrolyzer.not: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2. Pure water barely conducts electricity, so a little sulfuric acid is added as the electrolyte (it is not used up). Graphite electrodes, direct current from the dynamo. Hydrogen bubbles at the − electrode, oxygen at the +, twice as much hydrogen by volume. Splitting 2 mol of water takes ≈572 kJ: about 115 s at 5 kW.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: H2, made by splitting water. One bag ≈ 1 mol (≈24 L at 25 °C, 1 atm). 19th-century labs carried gases in rubberised-cloth bags. Store large amounts in a Gas Holder [6-02]. Later used as a protective furnace atmosphere and for ammonia (Haber–Bosch).
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note: O2, from the + electrode of the electrolyzer, half the volume of the hydrogen. One bag ≈ 1 mol. Keep it in a different holder from hydrogen: mixed, they make an explosive oxyhydrogen mixture. Later used for oxidising silicon (SiO2 film).
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_gas.note: The lightest gas. A balloon filled with it floats up into the sky.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_gas.note1: The gas that makes things burn. About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note1: In the age of gas lamps, gas tanks were sealed with water so the gas could not leak out.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note: A low-pressure tank: a bottomless iron bell over a tank of water (19th-century gasworks). Gas lifts the bell, and the bell's weight pushes the gas out. Holds one gas at a time (set by the first gas in, cleared when empty). Automatically takes the same gas from an adjacent electrolyzer. Capacity 1000 mol ≈ 24.5 m³ (25 °C, 1 atm). Mixing hydrogen and oxygen gives oxyhydrogen (2H2+O2→2H2O): bang.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note3: London's Gas Light and Coke Company (founded 1812) stored coal gas in water-sealed gasholders and piped it to street lamps. The huge cylindrical iron frames still stand at places like King's Cross, reused as a park and as flats.
block.semiconductor-lab.gas_holder.note4: Gas pressure = bell weight ÷ bell area (a few kPa, a few % above atmospheric), so no compressor is needed, but the volume stays large. Squeezing gas small enough to carry is the job of the compressor and cylinder [6-03]. Hydrogen molecules are tiny and slowly escape through gaps in metal and dissolve a little in the seal water (ignored in game).
item.minecraft.iron_ingot.placeholder: Approximation: the converter [1-26] treats a vanilla iron ingot as pig iron (≈4% carbon). To be replaced when the blast furnace [1-09] is added.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note1: Just blow air through iron and it becomes steel. The colour of the flame tells you when it's done.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note: Steel = iron with only about 0.1–0.5% carbon. Pig iron (≈4% C) is hard but brittle; nearly pure wrought iron is too soft. Steel, in between, is strong and tough. Made in the Bessemer converter by blowing air through molten pig iron, burning the carbon away: C+O2→CO2. Material for turbines, pressure vessels and lathes.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note3: Announced by Henry Bessemer (UK) in 1856. Steel had been a luxury made in small crucibles; a converter made several tonnes in about 20 minutes and the price of steel collapsed. Rails, bridges and ships turned to steel. William Kelly in the USA had noticed the same principle around the same time.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_ingot.note4: Early Bessemer steel kept oxygen and sulfur and was brittle. In 1856 Robert Mushet found that adding spiegeleisen (an Fe-Mn-C alloy) at the end removed the oxygen and restored the carbon (omitted: manganese is not in the mod yet). The acid lining could not remove phosphorus, so phosphorus-rich ores were useless until Thomas and Gilchrist's basic converter of 1878 [3-08].
block.semiconductor-lab.bessemer_convert: No fuel: just blow air through iron and it becomes steel.

A vessel that blows air up through molten pig iron from tuyeres in the bottom (Bessemer, 1856). No fuel: first the silicon, then the carbon burn, and that heat alone keeps the iron molten. The flame shows the progress: 1) red sparks (silicon) → 2) long white flame (the carbon "boil") → 3) the flame drops: done. In game: one iron ingot (≈ pig iron) + blower power 20 kW × 20 s → one steel ingot.

A real converter is a pear-shaped iron vessel tilted on trunnions to pour iron in and out. The blast came from a steam blowing engine. The lining is acidic silica refractory (here: refractory silica bricks [3-12]; early converters rammed ganister, a siliceous rock with clay).

Inside, mostly 2C+O2→2CO; at the mouth the CO burns in air to CO2, making the long flame. Si+O2→SiO2 releases a lot of heat, so low-silicon pig iron does not get hot enough. The end of the blow (flame drop) was judged by eye, later with a spectroscope watching the flame's light.
item.semiconductor-lab.refractory_brick_: Mostly quartz sand, shaped into a brick. It still has to be fired very hot.

Silica sand (SiO2) bound with a little slaked lime (about 2%, as milk of lime), pressed into shape. An ordinary furnace (~1000 C) is not hot enough: fire it in a blast furnace (~1450 C). During firing, quartz slowly turns into other crystal forms (tridymite, cristobalite), which is why silica bricks grow slightly instead of shrinking.
Ordinary bricks melt in a furnace. Only bricks full of quartz can take the heat.

Silica brick, about 95% SiO2. Fire-clay bricks soften around 1600 C, but silica bricks stay hard almost up to their melting point (~1700 C), so they were used for the roofs of steel furnaces. Silica is acidic: it is the right lining for an acid Bessemer converter.

1822: William Weston Young made bricks from the quartz-rich 'Dinas' rock of the Vale of Neath in Wales, so silica bricks are still called Dinas bricks. They made the hot open-hearth furnaces of the 1860s possible.

Silica bricks are acidic and are eaten by basic slag (CaO, MgO). That is why the Thomas converter (1878) needed a basic dolomite lining to remove phosphorus. Quartz changes crystal form near 573 C with a sudden size change, so silica bricks crack if heated or cooled quickly at low temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.galena.note: Lead sulfide PbS, the main ore of lead. Smelt it to roast it into lead oxide (PbO), then smelt that again to get lead. Galena often contains a little silver (0.01-1%); extracting it (cupellation [1-32]) is not implemented yet.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note1: Burning galena in air drives the sulfur out as a choking gas and leaves a yellow powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note: PbO, made by roasting galena in air: 2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2. Smelt it again: carbon and CO from the fuel take the oxygen away, PbO + C -> Pb + CO. In a furnace the SO2 escapes; roast in a reverberatory furnace [3-06] to collect it for sulfuric acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note3: Litharge is Greek for 'silver stone': it was the yellow crust left over when silver was separated from lead. It was also used in glazes, in lead glass [7-01] and in old paints.
item.semiconductor-lab.litharge.note4: Real roasting is done below the melting point of galena (about 600-800 C) with plenty of air, so the sulfur burns off without the ore melting. In real smelters, roasting and reduction are often joined (roast-reduction), and the SO2 is sent to an acid plant.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note1: The metal of old water pipes and printing type. It is bad for your body.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note: Pb. Soft, heavy (11.3 g/cm3) and melts at only 327 C, so people have smelted it since ancient times. It does not rust away in acid easily: used for sulfuric acid chambers [6-12], containers for hydrofluoric acid [2-10] and lead-acid batteries [4-07]. Lead is toxic: it builds up in the body and harms the brain and nerves.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note3: The Romans made water pipes from lead: the Latin word plumbum gave us 'plumbing' and the symbol Pb. Gutenberg's printing type (about 1450) was a lead-tin-antimony alloy. Leaded petrol and lead paint were banned in the 20th century because of lead poisoning.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_ingot.note4: Galena often contains silver. Lead was smelted first, then silver was separated by cupellation: melt the lead in air so it becomes PbO and soaks into a bone-ash dish, leaving only silver [1-32]. Much of the silver of the ancient world (and of Iwami in Japan) was made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_trioxide: A bright yellow powder. Tungsten is hiding inside it, bound to oxygen.
WO3. Reduce it with hydrogen in the hydrogen furnace: WO3 + 3H2 -> W + 3H2O (about 700-1000 C). Carbon is not used, because tungsten would grab the carbon and become tungsten carbide.

Placeholder: the real route fuses wolframite with soda (Na2CO3), dissolves sodium tungstate in water, precipitates tungstic acid with hydrochloric acid and roasts it to WO3 (iron and manganese are removed on the way). Soda [2-03] and HCl [6-06] are not implemented, so here the ore is simply roasted.

Tungsten was first isolated in 1783 by the Elhuyar brothers in Spain, from wolframite. The name wolfram (symbol W) comes from German miners: the ore 'ate' tin like a wolf when it was mixed in tin smelting.

Industrially the reduction goes step by step through blue and violet oxides (WO2.9, WO2.72, WO2) to W. The grain size of the powder is controlled by temperature, hydrogen flow and moisture: wet hydrogen gives coarse grains, dry hydrogen fine ones. Modern plants go through ammonium paratungstate (APT).
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_powder.n: Tungsten melts at about 3400 C. Nothing can melt it, so the powder is baked together.

Metal tungsten as a grey powder. No crucible survives 3400 C, so tungsten is made by powder metallurgy: press the powder into a bar and sinter it in hydrogen (hydrogen furnace: 2 powder + 1 H2 -> sintered bar).
Powder metallurgy is how the metals that are hardest to melt are made: tungsten, molybdenum [1-31], and tungsten-carbide cutting tools.

During sintering, atoms move across the contact points between grains (diffusion), so the gaps close and the bar shrinks by about 15% while becoming dense. The temperature must be close to the melting point for this to be fast.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_bar.note: A big electric current flowing through the bar itself heats it to about 3000 C.

Pressed tungsten powder sintered in hydrogen by passing a current straight through the bar (Coolidge's method). At this stage it is still brittle like glass. Hot swaging and wire drawing make it ductile. Craft it into tungsten wire.
Before Coolidge, tungsten filaments (Just and Hanaman, 1904) were squirted paste that broke easily. Coolidge found that working the hot metal again and again made it bendable at room temperature.

Swaging: the hot bar (about 1200-1500 C) is hammered thousands of times per minute by rotating dies, little by little thinner. The grains become long fibres, which is why worked tungsten is ductile but recrystallised tungsten (after overheating) becomes brittle again.
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.not: The thin wire that glows inside light bulbs and vacuum tubes.

Ductile tungsten wire (Coolidge, GE, 1909-1910). It does not melt even when glowing white-hot, so it is used for light-bulb filaments [B-01], vacuum-tube cathodes [5-02], X-ray tubes [B-03] and the needles of point-contact diodes [9-05].
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.pla: Approximation: swaging and drawing through diamond / tungsten-carbide dies are skipped (the bar becomes wire in the crafting grid).
item.semiconductor-lab.tungsten_wire.not: In 1910-1911 GE began selling lamps with drawn tungsten filaments. They gave about three times more light per watt than carbon filaments, and the tungsten bulb became the light of the 20th century.

Even tungsten slowly evaporates when it glows, darkening the glass and thinning the wire. Filling the bulb with argon (Langmuir 1913, from air separation [6-07]) slowed this down; halogen lamps go further by carrying evaporated tungsten back to the filament.
block.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_furnace: Tungsten is made by blowing hydrogen over hot yellow powder.

An electric furnace [4-12] with a steel tube of flowing hydrogen. 1) Reduction: WO3 + 3 H2 + 3 kW x 30 s -> tungsten powder. 2) Sintering: 2 tungsten powder + 1 H2 + 10 kW x 20 s -> sintered bar (current passed straight through the pressed bar). Hydrogen comes from bags in the lower-left slot, or automatically from a hydrogen gas holder next to it.

Hydrogen protects the hot metal from oxygen and takes the oxygen out of the oxide. The water vapour made by the reaction leaves with the gas stream; the exhaust hydrogen is burned at the furnace exit.

Hydrogen + air is explosive (4-75%), so real furnaces purge the air with nitrogen before letting hydrogen in, and keep a small flame burning at the exit. The same furnaces later reduced GeO2 for germanium and annealed metals.
item.semiconductor-lab.empty_gas_cylinde: A thick steel bottle that can hold gas squeezed to 150 times air pressure.

A seamless steel cylinder (about 10 L). Put it in a compressor next to a gas holder: it is filled with 50 mol of that gas at about 150 atm. Low-pressure bags (about 1 mol) are still handy for small amounts.

Gas cylinders became practical in the 1880s: Brin's Oxygen Company in London (1886) sold compressed oxygen in metal cylinders, and the Mannesmann brothers' seamless steel tubes (late 1880s) made strong cylinders without a welded seam.
50 mol at 25 C and 150 atm takes V = nRT/P = 50 x 0.0821 x 298 / 150, about 8 L (ideal gas). Real cylinders are tested with water at 5/3 of the filling pressure and re-tested every few years.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrogen_cylinder: In Japan, hydrogen cylinders are painted red so nobody mixes them up.
50 mol of H2 compressed to about 150 atm in a steel cylinder (about 1.2 m3 of gas at normal pressure). Flammable: 4-75% in air can explode.
Japan's High Pressure Gas Safety Act fixes cylinder colours: oxygen black, hydrogen red, carbon dioxide green, chlorine yellow, ammonia white, acetylene brown, others grey.

Hydrogen atoms are so small that they creep into steel and make it brittle (hydrogen embrittlement). Hydrogen cylinders use tougher, lower-strength steel, and modern 700-bar fuel-cell car tanks use carbon fibre with a plastic liner. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
item.semiconductor-lab.oxygen_cylinder.n: In Japan, oxygen cylinders are painted black.
50 mol of O2 compressed to about 150 atm. Pure oxygen makes things burn violently: never put oil or grease on the valve.
The first big use of bottled oxygen was the limelight of theatres (an oxy-hydrogen flame heating lime) and then welding and cutting with the oxy-acetylene torch (1903). Hospitals followed.

At high pressure, oil and grease can ignite by themselves in oxygen (adiabatic compression heats the gas when a valve is opened quickly). Oxygen valves are cleaned to remove oil and opened slowly. (The colours in this mod follow the Japanese standard - red for H2, black for O2. Other countries differ: in Europe (EN 1089-3) oxygen is white and hydrogen red; in the US colours are not fixed by law.)
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note1: High-pressure cylinders were made in the 1880s, and people could carry gas around.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note: An electric piston compressor. Place it next to a gas holder with at least 50 mol: empty cylinder + 50 mol + 5 kW x 124 s -> filled cylinder of that gas. The energy (620 kJ) is the work to squeeze 50 mol from 1 to 150 atm at constant temperature, nRT ln(150).
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note3: Squeezing gas heats it, so real compressors work in stages (for example 1 -> 6 -> 30 -> 150 atm) with water coolers between them. A bicycle pump gets warm for the same reason.
block.semiconductor-lab.compressor.note4: Isothermal work W = nRT ln(P2/P1) = 50 x 8.314 x 298 x ln150, about 621 kJ. Squeezing to 150 atm in one adiabatic stroke (no cooling) would need more work (about 1 MJ) and heat the gas to nearly 1000 C, which is why multi-stage cooling matters.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.n: A glass bell on an iron plate. Pump the air out with a hand pump next to it.

Holds a pressure (Pa). Starts at 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. A hand pump next to it lowers the pressure each stroke; air slowly leaks back in through the greased seal (1 Pa/s). You cannot see the pressure - use a mercury gauge.

19th-century labs used a glass bell jar ground flat at the rim and greased onto a flat plate. The outside air pushes the bell down with about 1 kg on every square centimetre, which is what keeps it sealed.
Large or hot chambers later became welded mild steel, and ultra-high vacuum uses stainless steel baked at 150-250 C so gas trapped in the walls comes out first. Here only the glass stage exists.
block.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber.p: Approximation: vanilla glass stands in for soda-lime glass [2-14] (not implemented) and the grease of the ground seal (tallow [2-09]) is left out.
message.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_chamber: You can't see air pressure. Hold a mercury vacuum gauge and right-click.
block.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pump: Magdeburg hemispheres: with the air pumped out, 16 horses could not pull them apart.

Otto von Guericke's air pump (c. 1650). Place next to a vacuum chamber and right-click with an empty hand: each stroke removes 20% of the air (chamber : cylinder = 4 : 1). It never gets below about 1 kPa (1/100 atm). Costs a little hunger.

Each stroke follows Boyle's law: the chamber air spreads into the empty cylinder, the valve closes, and that share is pushed outside. The pressure falls like 0.8, 0.64, 0.51... so the first strokes do the most.

The limit comes from dead volume: air left in the gap between the piston and the valve at the end of the stroke expands back in, and the leather packing leaks. Guericke reached roughly a few hundred Pa to 1 kPa. Better vacuum needed Sprengel's mercury pump (1865) and the diffusion pump (1915).
Approximation: the real cylinder was cast brass/bronze ([1-05] not implemented) - steel here. The leather packing uses vanilla leather (rubber [2-29] not implemented).
message.semiconductor-lab.hand_vacuum_pu: Place a vacuum chamber next to the pump.
Whoosh... the piston still moves easily (lots of air left)
Whoosh... very heavy - the air outside pushes back on the piston
It won't go lower - this is the hand pump's limit (about 1 kPa)
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnabar_dust.not: Red powder of mercury and sulfur. Roast it to get mercury.
Crushed cinnabar HgS (from a vanilla cinnabar block, 1 -> 2). Roast it: HgS + O2 -> Hg + SO2 at about 600 C. A furnace lets the SO2 escape; a reverberatory furnace collects it.
Cinnabar was also the red pigment vermilion. The Almaden mine in Spain was worked for over 2000 years and once produced a third of the world's mercury.

Roasting works because mercury boils at 357 C: it leaves the hot ore as vapour and condenses as liquid in the cool part of the retort. The sulfur leaves as SO2, which could become sulfuric acid [2-01].
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note1: The stuff inside old thermometers. Never touch it.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note: Hg, the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Made by roasting cinnabar dust in a furnace. Used for the mercury vacuum gauge; later for Sprengel and diffusion pumps and mercury lamps.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note3: Mercury is 13.6 times heavier than water, so a column only 76 cm tall balances the whole atmosphere. A water barometer would need about 10 m.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.note4: Mercury vapour is toxic and builds up in the body (Minamata disease was methylmercury). It was traded in iron flasks of 34.5 kg. Gallium [1-44] melts in your hand (30 C) but is solid at room temperature.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury.placehold: Omitted: the retort's condenser; the container (glass bottle / iron flask). In a furnace the SO2 escapes (a reverberatory furnace collects it). Warning only: real mercury vapour is poisonous.
item.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum_ga: Air pressure equals the weight of 76 cm of mercury.

A closed-end U-tube of mercury (Torricelli's mercury column, 1643). Right-click a vacuum chamber: the difference in mercury height is the pressure in mmHg (1 mmHg = 133 Pa, 1 atm = 760 mmHg). Below 1 mm it can't be read by eye.
One arm is sealed with nothing above the mercury (the 'Torricellian vacuum'); the other is open to the chamber. The chamber gas pushes its side down by exactly its pressure in mm of mercury.

For lower pressures came the McLeod gauge (1874, compresses a sample of gas with mercury so it can be read), the Pirani gauge (1906, how fast a hot wire cools) and the hot-cathode ionization gauge (1916, built like a vacuum tube).
Approximation: glass panes stand in for drawn glass tubing ([2-14] soda-lime glass not implemented); the scale board is sticks.
message.semiconductor-lab.mercury_vacuum: The mercury levels are within 1 mm - too low to read (below %s)
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube_assem: Everything is inside the glass, but it is still full of air. Seal it on a sealing station.
Glass bulb + tungsten wire filament + iron wire grid + iron plate. With air inside, the hot filament would burn out at once. Put it in a sealing station next to a pumped-down vacuum chamber.
Approximation: grid and plate are iron (nickel [1-37] not implemented). The lead-in wires through the glass (platinum / Dumet wire, glass-metal seal [5-12]) are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note1: Add one more electrode to a light bulb and you can control the flow of electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note: Lee de Forest's Audion (1906). The hot tungsten filament boils off electrons; the plate collects them; a small voltage on the grid between them controls a large current - an amplifier. Part of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note3: Fleming's diode (1904) used Edison's discovery that a hot filament gives off current. De Forest added the zig-zag grid. Before transistors, every radio, telephone repeater and early computer amplified with tubes like this.
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.note4: De Forest's first Audions were 'soft' - gas left inside made them erratic. Langmuir and Arnold (c. 1913) showed that a hard vacuum (about 10^-4 Pa) makes tubes stable, which needed diffusion pumps and getters (the silver film inside a tube is the getter that ate the last gas).
item.semiconductor-lab.vacuum_tube.place: PLACEHOLDER: sealed at 1.5 kPa because the hand pump can't go lower. A real tube needs about 0.1 Pa (soft) to 10^-4 Pa (hard) - Sprengel [5-15] / diffusion [5-05] pumps not implemented. Getter (Mg [1-39] / red phosphorus [5-16]) omitted.
Pump the air out of the bulb, then melt the glass neck shut.

Place next to a vacuum chamber (it is the exhaust manifold). Tube assembly + chamber at 1.5 kPa or lower + 500 W x 10 s (filament heated to drive out gas) -> triode vacuum tube. Each tube lets some air back into the chamber (5% of the gap to 1 atm) - pump again.

Real tube factories pumped each bulb through a glass tube at its top, heated the parts to drive out gas, then melted that tube shut with a flame. The little glass tip on old tubes and light bulbs is where it was sealed off.

Gas hides in the metal and glass surfaces. While pumping, the filament is run hot and the plate heated (later by induction) so the gas comes out before sealing; finally the getter is flashed to absorb what is left.
Approximation: the sealing flame (gas torch) is represented by electric power; threshold 1.5 kPa is far too high (see Triode Vacuum Tube).
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note1: A glass jar wrapped in metal inside and out stores electricity.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note: The first capacitor (Kleist and Musschenbroek, 1745): metal foil on the inside and outside of a glass jar, the glass between them as insulator. Charge piles up on the two foils. With a coil it forms the tuned circuit of the HF oscillator.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note3: Early radio transmitters used racks of Leyden jars as their capacitors. A coil (L) and a capacitor (C) together ring at one frequency, f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC)) - the same idea as tuning a radio.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.note4: Musschenbroek got such a shock from his jar that he wrote he would not repeat it for the whole kingdom of France. Benjamin Franklin later showed the charge sits on the glass surfaces, not in the water the first jars held.
item.semiconductor-lab.leyden_jar.placeh: Approximation: the foil was tin foil (tin [1-30] not implemented) - copper here (copper-foil capacitors are real too). Vanilla glass bottle.
item.semiconductor-lab.hf_oscillator.not: The machine that makes transistors ran on vacuum tubes - the very parts transistors would replace.

Two triode tubes + coil + Leyden jar + power input. The tubes keep the coil-capacitor circuit ringing at radio frequency (hundreds of kHz) and feed it to the induction coil of the zone refining furnace, where eddy currents melt only the germanium.

A tube amplifier whose output is fed back to its own grid keeps itself oscillating (Meissner and Armstrong, 1912-1913). Induction heaters of the 1950s that melted germanium were exactly such tube oscillators, with big water-cooled triodes.

Bell Labs' zone refiners (Pfann, 1952) were heated by RF induction of a few hundred kHz to MHz. Only the material inside the coil heats, so the graphite boat and quartz tube stay cooler - a clean way to melt one narrow zone.
block.semiconductor-lab.electric_furnace: It heats things with electricity instead of fire, so no smoke gets in.

Resistance furnace: current through graphite rods turns into heat (Joule heat, P = I squared R), up to about 1500 C. 5 kW x 10 s per item. Fires refractory bricks and clay-graphite boats. With a hydrogen tube added it becomes the hydrogen furnace.
Nichrome wire (1906) needs nickel and chromium, which we don't have yet - but a graphite rod works as a heating element too. 1500 C is above the melting point of silicon (1414 C).
Omitted: hot graphite burns in air (C + O2 -> CO2), so real graphite-element furnaces run under inert gas or vacuum, and the rods are consumables. Here the rods never wear out.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: A stick of graphite. Electricity flows through it and makes it glow hot.
Heating element of the electric furnace [4-12] and electrode of the Acheson furnace [3-10]. Graphite conducts electricity but has some resistance, so current turns into heat.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.plac: Approximation: real carbon rods (arc lamp carbons, 19th c.) are carbon powder bound with pitch (coal tar) and baked. Pitch is not implemented, so 3 natural graphite make 2 rods.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_rod.note: Graphite's resistance falls as it gets hotter (unlike metals), and it does not melt at normal pressure - it sublimes near 3600 C. That is why graphite heaters can go far above any metal wire.
Bake charcoal with electricity way too hard and it turns into graphite.

Resistance furnace where the charge itself is the heater: current flows from graphite electrodes straight through the packed carbon. 4 coal/charcoal + 1 sand -> 2 synthetic graphite, after the furnace reaches 2500 C. Needs 500 kW (about 10 steam engines); with less power it settles at a lower temperature and never graphitizes.

Edward Acheson found silicon carbide (carborundum) in 1891 while trying to make diamonds, and patented synthetic graphite in 1896. Heated far enough, SiC loses its silicon as vapour and leaves graphite behind - he thought the sand acted as a catalyst.

Game model: temperature rises with power in and falls with heat lost (proportional to temperature above 20 C), tuned so 500 kW settles at 2600 C. Real furnaces were tens of metres long, ran on Niagara hydroelectric power at hundreds of kW to MW, and one cycle took days. Today it is known that soft carbons (petroleum coke) graphitize without any catalyst.
item.semiconductor-lab.synthetic_graphit: Graphite made by people. Purer than the graphite you dig up.

Made in the Acheson furnace above 2500 C. At that heat the carbon atoms rearrange into graphite layers, and impurities (ash, sulfur, metals) boil away. Machined into high-purity boats for zone refining.

Natural graphite carries the minerals it grew in (clay, iron, silica). Synthetic graphite became the standard for electrodes, crucibles and later nuclear reactor moderators (the 1942 Chicago Pile used hundreds of tonnes).

Graphitization: carbon atoms in coke are arranged in small, misaligned layers. Above about 2500 C they move enough to stack into the ordered hexagonal layers of graphite. Electrical resistance drops and the material becomes soft and slippery.
item.semiconductor-lab.graphite_boat.not: The old 19th-century kind: cheap, but clay impurities seep into the germanium, so it only gets you to 9N.

Clay-graphite crucibles (natural graphite bonded with clay) were the standard for melting metals in the 19th century. For semiconductors the clay (aluminium, iron, alkali metals) is the problem - Bell Labs used high-purity synthetic graphite.
item.semiconductor-lab.synthetic_graphit: A boat carved from very clean man-made graphite. Germanium gets all the way to 10N.
Goes in the middle slot of the zone refining furnace and is not used up. With this boat germanium refines to 10N (the clay-graphite boat stops at 9N).
Molten germanium does not wet or react with graphite, so a clean graphite boat adds almost nothing to the bar. Pfann's zone refiners used high-purity graphite boats inside a quartz tube.

Omitted: real boats are machined on a lathe/mill from a graphite block, then purified further by baking in chlorine or freon gas at about 2500 C (metal impurities leave as volatile chlorides). Here 3 synthetic graphite are shaped at the crafting table.
block.semiconductor-lab.zone_refining_fu: Melt only a thin slice of the bar and slide it along: the dirt follows the melt to the end.

Left: germanium (max 8). Middle: graphite boat (not used up; clay-graphite = up to 9N, synthetic = up to 10N). Right: dopant. Runs on electricity: the built-in HF oscillator draws 3 kW (stops without power). 30 s per pass.

The HF oscillator drives the copper coil; the alternating magnetic field induces currents in the germanium itself, so only the part inside the coil melts. The boat and the quartz tube stay cool enough not to contaminate it.
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.no_boat: Put a graphite boat in the middle
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.need_power: No power: the HF oscillator is off
gui.semiconductor-lab.refiner.clay_cap: Clay boat stops at 9N. 10N: synthetic boat
item.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_dyna: A dynamo with no magnet inside. It makes its own magnet out of its own electricity.

Siemens 1866: a steel core + 4 coils. Right-click a water wheel or steam engine to swap out its permanent-magnet dynamo: output x2 (a steam engine also burns coal twice as fast — same electricity per coal, twice the power per machine).

The core keeps a little leftover magnetism. Spinning makes a weak current, which goes through the field coils and makes the field stronger, which makes more current... it builds itself up in seconds (the 'dynamo-electric principle').

Permanent magnets of the 1860s were weak, so magneto machines could only turn part of the engine's power into electricity. Electromagnet fields made big generators possible — Wheatstone and Varley found the same idea in the same months. Energy is still conserved: double the electricity needs double the steam.
message.semiconductor-lab.self_excited_d: Installed the self-excited dynamo: output x2
This generator already has a self-excited dynamo
This generator already has an electromagnet field built in
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.no: Steam spins a fan really fast. This is how most power plants still work.

Parsons 1884. Coal + water -> 500 kW. One coal lasts 18 s (9 MJ = 30% of the coal's heat; the steam engine gets 5%). Water: a bucket in the top slot (1 bucket = 2 coal), or a water source block beside it feeds it forever. Enough to run the Acheson furnace (500 kW) by itself.

No piston going back and forth, just a wheel of blades turning in one direction — so it can spin fast (Parsons' first: 18,000 rpm) and be built huge. Power plants sit by rivers and the sea because they need lots of cooling water.

Real plants are multi-stage (steam expands through many rows of blades) and use a condenser to turn the steam back into water under vacuum, which raises efficiency. Coal plants reach about 33-40% today, combined-cycle gas plants over 60%. Your electricity is still mostly made by spinning turbines.
block.semiconductor-lab.steam_turbine.pl: Simplified: blades are not machined on a lathe ([8-01] not yet implemented); single stage, no condenser; feedwater from a river is not used up.
block.semiconductor-lab.lead_acid_batter: The same kind of battery as in a car. It stores electricity as a chemical change.

Planté 1859. Lead plates in sulfuric acid. Holds 1 MJ. Every face both charges and discharges (up to 10 kW each; only 85% of the charge is stored). On a cable network it charges when there is spare power and discharges when machines need more. Keeps its charge when broken. Right-click: charge level. Glows while discharging.

Charging: 2PbSO4 + 2H2O -> Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. Discharging runs it backwards, so the acid gets weaker as the battery empties — mechanics check charge by measuring the acid's density. Planté made the PbO2 plate by charging and discharging bare lead sheets over and over ('forming').

The first rechargeable battery, and still in nearly every car 160+ years later because it can give a huge current to the starter motor and is cheap and recyclable (over 95% of the lead is recycled). Pure lead plates are soft, so grids were hardened with a few % antimony ([1-43]). Overcharging splits water into H2 + O2 — battery rooms need ventilation.
Simplified: no self-discharge, no voltage (12 V etc.); the case is glass (real: glass jars, later hard rubber / plastic).
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note1: A waxy, glowing element. It catches fire by itself in air, so it is kept under water.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note2: White phosphorus, P4 (Wöhler process: bone ash + sand + carbon). Burns spontaneously in air at about 30 C and glows in the dark (slow oxidation). Real labs store it under water. Used here as the n-type dopant.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note3: Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus in 1669 by boiling down urine — the first element found by a known person. The name means 'light-bearer' in Greek because it glows.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus.note4: White phosphorus is P4 tetrahedra and is very toxic (the 'phossy jaw' disease of match-factory workers). Heating it to about 250 C without air turns it into red phosphorus, a stable polymer used on matchbox strikers and as a getter in vacuum tubes [5-16] (red phosphorus is not in the mod yet). Germanium was doped with Sb/As at first; phosphorus became the main n-type dopant for silicon.
message.semiconductor-lab.cable.network: Cable network: %s cables, longest path %s (loss %s%%), %s generators, %s machines, %s batteries, %s delivered
block.semiconductor-lab.copper_cable.not: Joins machines into one electric grid. Long cables lose more power.

Real loss is P = I^2 R: doubling the voltage halves the current for the same power and cuts the loss to a quarter. That is why power lines run at hundreds of kV (transformer [4-10]). In this mod the whole network shares one 1 MW limit (like one trunk line) and the loss uses the longest path for every machine - both are simplifications.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note1: Burn seashells or white stone and you get lime: the start of wall plaster.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note: CaO. Calcite (CaCO3) heated to about 900 C loses its carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. A furnace (~1000 C) or blast furnace is hot enough. Seashells and limestone are also CaCO3 and burn the same way.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note3: Lime plaster is one of the oldest man-made materials: floors at Catalhoyuk and other early villages (around 9000-7000 BC) were coated with burnt lime. People built lime kilns everywhere there was limestone or shells.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note4: Above about 900 C the pressure of CO2 released by CaCO3 exceeds 1 atm, so the reaction runs on its own. Burned too hot or too long, lime becomes 'dead-burned' (dense crystals that react slowly with water). The CO2 from lime kilns is still a big part of the cement industry's emissions.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.placeho: Omitted: the CO2 given off is not collected (a furnace has only one output).
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note1: Pour water on quicklime and it gets hot enough to steam, then falls into a white powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note: Ca(OH)2. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 gives off a lot of heat. Mixed as 'milk of lime' (about 2%), it binds silica sand into Dinas refractory bricks. In air it slowly takes back CO2: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, which is how lime plaster hardens.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note3: The Romans mixed slaked lime with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and got a concrete that sets even under water. Japanese castle walls (shikkui plaster) are slaked lime with seaweed glue and fibres.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note4: Slaking releases about 65 kJ per mole of CaO, enough to boil water or set wood on fire; self-heating meal boxes still use this reaction. Slaked lime is a strong base (pH about 12.4) used to causticize potash [2-02] and soda [2-08] and to neutralize acids.
block.semiconductor-lab.reverberatory_fu: Roasting ore sends its sulfur up the chimney as smoke. It used to be poison gas; collected, it becomes sulfuric acid.

Burns coal or charcoal (1 piece = 8 roasts, 10 s each) and roasts sulfide ores in air without melting them. Galena -> lead oxide + SO2; cinnabar dust -> mercury + SO2; sphalerite -> zinc oxide + SO2, plus germanium concentrate every 4th and indium every 8th. SO2 + water -> sulfuric acid.

The fire burns in a separate firebox; the flame and hot gas sweep over the hearth and the low roof reflects ('reverberates') the heat down onto the ore. English smelters used it for lead and copper from the 1690s, and Henry Cort used it for puddling iron in 1784. The Nirayama reverberatory furnace in Japan (Egawa Hidetatsu, finished by his son Hidetoshi in 1857) cast cannons and is a World Heritage site.

Because the fuel never touches the ore, the ash and sulfur of coal do not get into the metal. Roasting itself gives off heat (sulfur burns), so little fuel is needed. Smelter smoke (SO2) once killed forests around mines, such as Ashio in Japan; today smelter gas is sent to contact-process sulfuric acid plants, and smelters are major acid producers.

Approximation: a real furnace is a large brick building (firebox, hearth, flue, chimney); shrunk to one block. Ge and In really come from zinc-refining residues (leach residue, flue dust), not straight from roasting; here they come out as roasting by-products.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note1: A white powder: old white paint (zinc white) and the white in sunscreen.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note: ZnO, made by roasting sphalerite: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2. Smelt it to reduce it with the fuel's carbon: ZnO + C -> Zn + CO.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note3: Zinc white became an artists' paint in 1834 ('Chinese white', Winsor & Newton). Unlike lead white it is not poisonous and does not darken.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.note4: ZnO is itself a semiconductor (band gap about 3.3 eV). It absorbs UV, which is why it is in sunscreen, and it is used in varistors (surge protectors) and transparent electronics.
item.semiconductor-lab.zinc_oxide.placeh: Approximation: reducing ZnO needs about 1000 C, above zinc's boiling point (907 C), so real zinc escapes as vapour and must be condensed (distillation smelting [1-13]). Done in one furnace step here.
